verdict.summary:
ANSWER

The permanent-removal temperature for fiber core wire rope slings is 200 °F; the maximum use temperature for polypropylene web slings is also 200 °F. The difference is therefore 200 °F − 200 °F = 0 °F. The fiber core wire rope sling limit is not higher at all — the two limits are numerically identical under 29 CFR 1910.184.

1. THE TWO STATED LIMITS (verbatim, 29 CFR 1910.184)

(a) Wire rope slings — 'Safe operating temperatures', subparagraph (3):
    'Fiber core wire rope slings of all grades shall be permanently removed from service if they are exposed to temperatures in excess of 200 °F. When nonfiber core wire rope slings of any grade are used at temperatures above 400 °F or below minus 60 °F, recommendations of the sling manufacturer regarding use at that temperature shall be followed.'
    → fiber core wire rope sling permanent-removal threshold = 200 °F.

(b) Synthetic web slings — 'Safe operating temperatures', subparagraph (7):
    'Synthetic web slings of polyester and nylon shall not be used at temperatures in excess of 180 °F. Polypropylene web slings shall not be used at temperatures in excess of 200 °F.'
    → polypropylene web sling maximum use temperature = 200 °F.

2. CALCULATION

    ΔT = T(fiber core wire rope, permanent removal) − T(polypropylene web, max use)
       = 200 °F − 200 °F
       = 0 °F

    Units: both limits are stated in degrees Fahrenheit in the regulation itself, so no conversion (no Celsius→Fahrenheit step, no rounding) is involved. The result is exact, not an approximation.

3. INTERPRETATION AND COMPARABILITY

Both provisions are phrased as strict upper bounds ('in excess of 200 °F'). At exactly 200 °F, neither limit is exceeded: a fiber core wire rope sling need not be permanently removed and a polypropylene web sling may still be used. Above 200 °F, both are simultaneously non-compliant. Consequently there is no temperature band in which a polypropylene web sling is permitted while a fiber core wire rope sling must already have been removed — the two thresholds coincide.

The question compares two different kinds of limit (a permanent-removal trigger versus a maximum-use prohibition). That difference in kind does not affect the arithmetic here, because the numeric thresholds are equal; the answer would be the same under any consistent reading of the two sentences. It would matter only if one were asking which limit governs conduct — and the answer to that is: above 200 °F both govern, and the fiber core wire rope sling must be destroyed while the polypropylene sling must simply be taken out of service.

4. DISTRACTOR VALUES EXPLICITLY EXCLUDED

  • 180 °F — the polyester/nylon synthetic web sling limit (same subparagraph (7)); not polypropylene. Using it would wrongly give 20 °F.
  • 400 °F and −60 °F — the nonfiber core wire rope sling referral thresholds in subparagraph (3); not the fiber-core removal temperature. Using 400 °F would wrongly give 200 °F.
  • 1000 °F — the alloy steel chain sling heat-removal threshold ('Employers must permanently remove an alloy steel-chain slings from service if it is heated above 1000 degrees F'); a different sling type entirely.
  • 180 °F / −20 °F — the natural and synthetic fiber rope sling working-load-limit temperature range ('minus 20 °F to plus 180 °F'); a different sling type.

5. VERSION / AS-OF-DATE VERIFICATION (2026-11-21)

Both provisions were read from the following authoritative sources, and are word-for-word identical across them:
  • eCFR, 29 CFR subtitle B, chapter XVII, part 1910, subpart N, § 1910.184 (current text; fetched 2026-11-23T21:18:53Z; sha256 0b902b30fd4e)
  • OSHA standard number page for 1910.184 (fetched 2026-11-23T21:18:52Z; sha256 0b902b30fd4e)
  • GovInfo, CFR-2025-title29-vol5, § 1910.184 XML (fetched 2026-11-23T21:18:52Z; sha256 6a920b6ebc04)

Because the eCFR 'current' text as of 2026-11-23 is identical to the 2025 annual print edition for both provisions, no amendment to these paragraphs took effect between the 2025 edition and the requested as-of date of 2026-11-21. The regulation does not incorporate ASME B30.9 or another external standard by reference in a way that changes these two numeric temperature limits; the numbers appear as plain text in § 1910.184 itself. The answer is therefore stable across the requested date.

Residual risk (stated for completeness, not as a blocker): the as-of date is two days earlier than the fetch date, so the verification is by identity with the current text rather than by a point-in-time query; an amendment published and effective within that 48-hour window would not be caught, but the match with the 2025 print edition makes such a change to these two sentences essentially implausible.

6. CITATION NOTE

The subparagraph numbers (3) under 'Wire rope slings' and (7) under 'Synthetic web slings' are taken directly from the fetched regulatory text. The lettered paragraph designators (commonly cited as § 1910.184(e)(3) and § 1910.184(i)(7)) are not reproduced in the fetched excerpts and are not relied on here; the numeric answer of 0 °F depends only on the quoted sentences and their subparagraph numbers.

7. BOTTOM LINE FOR THE SAFETY FILE

Both the fiber core wire rope sling permanent-removal threshold and the polypropylene web sling maximum use temperature are 200 °F under 29 CFR 1910.184 as in force on 2026-11-21. The difference is 0 °F. Any sling-operation procedure written against this regulation should use a single 200 °F ceiling for both sling types, with the additional consequence that a fiber core wire rope sling exposed above 200 °F must be permanently removed from service, not merely set aside.

quotes.whole: The time of concentration (defined in Section 2.5.1) varies with the size and shape of the drainage area, the land slope, the type of surface, the intensity of rainfall, and whether flow is overland or channelized. The time of concentration can be considered the sum of an overland flow time and the travel times in gutters, swales, storm drains, etc. Technically, the time of concentration is the travel time of a wave, as opposed to the actual water velocity, from the most hydraulically remote point to the point in question. However, uncertainties about the actual overland flow path, roughness, slope and rainfall variations (temporal and spatial) limit both the need for making this distinction and the accuracy of any calculation.(5) Extreme precision is not warranted in determining time of concentration, particularly for small area drainage facility design; however, since the peak discharge (Q) is generally quite sensitive to the time of concentration, care should be taken to insure an appropriate value is obtained.

quotes.whole: After adjusting inlet locations the storm drain laterals and main line can be sized. Laterals are sized based on the discharge used to size the inlets. However, the discharge for the main line is not simply the sum of the incremental discharges at each inlet. Recalling that in the Rational Method the rainfall intensity used should be based on the longest time of concentration to the design point, the discharge for the main line should be determined based on longest time of concentration from various upstream approach branches and the corresponding accumulated CA values. This procedure satisfies the assumptions and stipulations for use of the Rational Method.

The assumptions in the Rational Formula are as follows:
1. Drainage area should be smaller than 300 acres.
2. Peak flow occurs when all of the watershed is contributing.

verdict.summary:
HYDRAULICS ENGINEER — ANSWER TO BOTH ASKS (FHWA HDS-4, rational method)

ANSWER 1 — Minimum time of concentration for selecting rainfall intensity: 5 minutes.

Source wording (HDS-4, rational-method section, time of concentration):
- "A minimum time of concentration of 5 minutes is recommended for finding the intensity used for estimating the design discharge." (HDS-4, Sec. 2.4-2, Time of Concentration)
- Same rule in the later (Pub. No. FHWA-08-090, 2008) revision, Ch. 2: "As a general guideline, if the total time of concentration is less than 5 minutes, a minimum value of 5 minutes should be used for estimating the design discharge."

Application rule: compute tc by summing overland (sheet) flow + shallow concentrated flow + channel/pipe travel times to the design point. If the sum is < 5 min, enter i–D–F curves at 5 min, not at the computed value. Rationale given in HDS-4: Q is quite sensitive to tc at small tc, and the intensity–duration curve steepens sharply below ~5 min, so computed intensities there are unreliable and would over-predict Q. Note that the 5-min floor is a general guideline, not a physical constant; it is applied to the duration used to read intensity, and the same 5-min tc is used for the C and CA accumulation.

ANSWER 2 — Approximate maximum drainage area for which the rational method is recommended: 200 acres (about 80 hectares in SI).

Source wording:
- "The method is recommended for use in determining the design discharge for roadside drainage channels draining less than about 200 acres." (HDS-4, Sec. 2.4)
- "For the design of highway drainage structures, the use of the rational method should be restricted to drainage areas less than 200 acres unless no other method is available to estimate the design discharge." (HDS-4, Sec. 2.4)
- SI text of the same document: "For the design of highway drainage structures, the use of the rational method should be restricted to drainage areas less than 80 hectares." (80 ha ≈ 198 acres; the 200-acre and 80-hectare figures are the same limit in dual units, rounded.)

So the paired figures are 200 acres / 80 hectares, "less than about" — i.e., a practical upper bound on applicability, not a hard regulatory cap; beyond it HDS-4 directs the designer to another method (e.g., TR-55/SCS graphical peak discharge, or a routed hydrograph method) unless no alternative exists.

EDITION / PROVENANCE NOTES (values reported above are edition-stable)
- Both the archived HDS-4 ('Introduction to Highway Hydraulics' lineage, Sec. 2.4/2.4-2) and the 2008 HDS-4 revision (FHWA-08-090, Ch. 2, Secs. 2.5.3–2.5.5) carry the 5-minute minimum; the 2008 text phrases it as a floor applied when the computed tc is less than 5 minutes. The 200-acre restriction appears in the HDS-4 rational-method text and in the SI (hectare) version as 80 ha. The 2008 revision's dual-unit presentation (SI primary, English in parentheses) does not change either figure.
- Do not confuse these with other FHWA documents: HEC-19 lists "drainage area should be smaller than 300 acres" among the rational-formula assumptions. That 300-acre figure is HEC-19, not HDS-4, and is not the answer to ask 2.
- Jurisdictional manuals commonly tighten these values and govern over HDS-4 where adopted. Example (MDOT Roadway Design Drainage Manual, Nov. 2025): minimum tc = 5 min for paved areas other than bridge decks, 10 min for bridge decks, 10 min for overland (sheet) flow and unpaved roads; rational method limited to 200 acres or less. Where a state manual applies, use its minimum tc — HDS-4's 5 min is the floor, not a ceiling on local requirements.

PRACTICAL USE STATEMENT
For a design point: (1) delineate A; if A ≥ ~200 acres (80 ha), stop and use an alternative method unless none is available, in which case document the exception; (2) compute tc by path summation; (3) set tc = max(tc,computed, 5 min); (4) read i for the design frequency at duration = tc; (5) Q = Ku·C·i·A with Ku = 1 (English, i in in/hr, A in acres) or 0.278 (SI, i in mm/h, A in ha). For complex areas, check partial-area peaks using the shorter tc of the impervious subarea in addition to the full-area peak — HDS-4 explicitly warns the maximum Q may come from a subarea at higher intensity (e.g., 20.0 of 21.4 acres at 5 min governing over the 14-min full-area peak).

verdict.summary:
# Compliance-file citation review: NIST/NBS TN 904 as a source for design basic wind speed

## 1. Question and disposition

A compliance file cites NIST Technical Note 904, *Correlation of Floor Vibration to Human Response*, for a **design basic wind speed**. Two determinations are made, from the supplied page passages only:

1. **Verdict (ask 2): NO.** TN 904 cannot be used as the source for a design basic wind speed. It is a floor-vibration/human-response research note and contains no wind speed data of any kind. The compliance-file citation is an error and must be replaced.
2. **Value (ask 3): 25 Hz** — the cut-off frequency of the accelerometer's signal-conditioning equipment in the report's Appendix A field test. It is an instrumentation bandwidth statement, not a wind speed and not a structural acceptance criterion.

## 2. Source identification

- James R. Shaver, *Correlation of Floor Vibration to Human Response*, National Bureau of Standards (now NIST) **Technical Note 904**, published January 1, 1976, report number NBS TN 904, DOI 10.6028/NBS.TN.904 (NIST publication record; PDF at nvlpubs.nist.gov).
- Documentation nuance to record in the file: the GovInfo copy of the same title/author is catalogued as **NBSIR 75-951**, issued 1975, DOI 10.6028/NBS.IR.75-951. The 25 Hz passage is verbatim identical in both fetched copies, so the report-number discrepancy does not affect either finding; it only needs to be noted so the file cites one identified edition consistently.

## 3. What the document is about (evidence in the passages)

- Abstract: "A new approach to the problem of perceptible floor vibrations is presented based on the assumption that human activity, which produces the vibration, and human response to vibration are random variables. Techniques for data reduction are discussed... Data from floor vibrations is compared with current criteria for human response." Key words: "Analysis; experimental; floor systems; human response; random process; spectral analysis; vibration."
- Section list: Introduction; Background; Approach to Problem; Data Reduction and Analysis; Damping; Human Response to Vibration; Summary; References; Appendix A: Field Test; Appendix B: Computer Program.
- Engineering scope: serviceability design of floor systems by deflection limits; dynamic characteristics of floors; the forcing function is **human activity** (walking etc.); response treated as a random process: "F(t) + G(t) -> Y(t) => D(t)" where F(t) is the random forcing function, G(t) the deterministic floor characteristics, Y(t) the random floor response, D(t) the random human response.
- Human-response criteria: the note compares results to ISO/DIS 2631, "allowable rms accelerations at different frequencies for various levels of exposure time... primarily intended for periodic (sinusoidal) vibrations in the frequency range from 1 Hz to 80 Hz"; standard acceleration levels are set per direction of vibration and weighted for vibration input type, occupant classification and time condition.
- Field test (Appendix A): wood-joist floor instrumented with an LVDT at mid-span of the clear span and an accelerometer on the floor above it; reported peak rms acceleration of 0.95 mg from a 40-second continuous walking test record; accelerometer range 0.001 mg to 10 mg.

**Wind content audit.** The supplied passages contain no occurrence of wind speed, design basic wind speed, wind loading, wind pressure, meteorological data, return period, risk category, exposure category, or any velocity expressed in mph, m/s, or knots. The only quantitative content is vibrational (Hz), acceleration (mg), and duration (s). There is therefore no passage from which a design basic wind speed could be read, quoted, or derived.

## 4. What a design basic wind speed source must provide, and why TN 904 fails that test

A defensible design basic wind speed citation must supply, at minimum: (a) the governing standard and **edition** (e.g., the wind-load provisions of the governing building code, typically the IBC-referenced ASCE 7 wind chapter, or a jurisdictional amendment); (b) the map/table/figure and section number from which the site value is read; (c) the site location; (d) the quantity's definition — a nominal gust speed at a stated reference height above ground in a stated exposure, with a stated probability/return period and risk category; and (e) the numeric value with units (commonly mph or m/s).

TN 904 provides **none** of these elements: it is not a wind-loading, meteorological, or code document; it is a 1970s serviceability research report on floor vibration; and it contains no wind data at all. It therefore cannot serve as the source even indirectly.

**Disposition:** the compliance-file citation is a citation error — most plausibly a wrong-document citation or a misattributed value. Corrective action:
1. Flag the TN 904 citation as an invalid source for design basic wind speed and log the discrepancy (citation/content mismatch) in the file's review record.
2. Replace it with the wind-speed provision of the **governing code/standard edition**, recording: edition year, section/map/table number, site location, risk category, reference height, exposure, return period, the value, and its units.
3. The specific numeric wind speed cannot be taken from TN 904 or from anything quoted inside it; it must come from the code edition and site data identified above.
4. If TN 904 is cited elsewhere in the file for floor-vibration serviceability or human response to vibration, retain it there — that is its actual subject.

## 5. The 25 Hz passage — verbatim text and what it actually says

**Verbatim (Appendix A, field-test instrumentation):**

> "The range of the accelerometer is from 10 mg to 0.001 mg. Figure 6 shows the location of this instrumentation. The LVDT was positively attached to the joist at mid-point of the clear span and the accelerometer set on the floor directly above the LVDT. Output from the LVDT and accelerometer were recorded as analog signals. While the frequency response of the electronic equipment was adequate to reproduce the time histories, the signal conditioning equipment for the accelerometer has a cut-off frequency of 25 Hz. This is generally considered satisfactory for most wood-joist floor systems."

**Meaning:** the 25 Hz figure is the **cut-off frequency of the accelerometer's signal-conditioning equipment**, i.e. an instrumentation bandwidth limit of the measurement chain used in the report's field test. The report states the equipment's frequency response was adequate to reproduce the measured time histories and that the 25 Hz cut-off "is generally considered satisfactory for most wood-joist floor systems."

**What it is not:**
- It is **not** a design basic wind speed (it is a frequency, in Hz, not a velocity).
- It is **not** a floor natural-frequency design limit or an acceptance criterion; the note's structural floor properties are described as deterministic engineering characteristics, with no 25 Hz limit imposed on floors.
- It is **not** a human-response threshold; the note's human-response criteria are allowable rms accelerations versus frequency and exposure time per ISO/DIS 2631, whose stated band is 1 Hz to 80 Hz.
- It **is** a statement about the accelerometer signal conditioning in the Appendix A field test, qualified by "generally considered satisfactory for most wood-joist floor systems."

## 6. Numeric consistency check

- 25 Hz (instrumentation cut-off) lies within the 1 Hz to 80 Hz range of ISO/DIS 2631 cited in the human-response section; no conflict is created by treating it as a measurement-chain bandwidth.
- Reported peak rms acceleration 0.95 mg lies within the accelerometer's stated 0.001 mg to 10 mg range.
- No value stated in this document is used as a wind speed, and no stated value violates any limit quoted in the same document.

## 7. Result values

- Ask 2 — can TN 904 be the source for a design basic wind speed? **No** (identifier verdict, no unit).
- Ask 3 — what does the 25 Hz passage actually say? **25 Hz** = the cut-off frequency of the accelerometer's signal-conditioning equipment in the Appendix A field test, described as generally satisfactory for most wood-joist floor systems (unit: Hz).

during the past decade on the various aspects of vibrating floor systems have
increased the awareness of the engineering community to the fact that the traditional
serviceability design procedure does not necessarily lead to floor systems with
satisfactory dynamic characteristics which prevents objectionable vibrations
from the occupant viewpoint when the floor is subjected to human activitv.
Recent efforts [4.5] to study the problem of perceptible floor vibrations
have primarily employed experimental techniques. Results from these studies
have been inconclusive as to what constitutes objectio

vibrations based on the assumption that human activity and human response to
2/ vibration are random variables. Presented is a random varxable methodology-based on physical testing and subsequent analysis of the dynamic response of
floor systems subjected to human activity.
2 . BACKGROUND
In order to understand why both human activity and occupant response
should be characterized as random variables, it is necessary to understand
the difference between a deterministic variable and one that is random. A
deterministic variable is one whose value can be calculated or determined
from knowledge of
Correlation of Floor Vibration to Human Response
National Bureau of Standards Technical Note 904

The human response to vibration involves many variables: vibration input where intensity, frequency, direction and duration must be considered; psychological influences in the form of mental state, motivation and exper-ience; and physical influences from sound and sight. Given this multiplicity of parameters, it is reasonable to classify human response as a random process.

It should be pointed out that the structural floor systems are not considered to be a random variable. Although there are several types of floor systems, their dynamic properties can be described deterministically from an engineering viewpoint. Rather it is the forcing function (human activity) and the human response to this activity which must be considered as random processes. This makes the overall problem of human response to floor vibration induced by human activity a random vibration problem. This can be stated in functional form as: F(t) + G(t) -> Y(t) =5> D(t) where F(t) is the random

The primary approach to obtaining a meaningful dynamic response of a floor system subjected to human activity is to first obtain a time history and then transform this time history into the frequency domain using Fourier techniques. In addition, the mean square value and probability density function should be obtained. It does not appear at this time that the autocorrelation function or the power spectral density function will provide any useful information.

The most useful output from the Fourier spectrum is the modulus. This modulus is obtained by realizing that the Fourier spectrum can be represented by a complex expression. X(f) = |x(f)| e^ 6(f) (4 - 10) where |x(f) | is the modulus and e -1 is the phase.
The phase presentation of the spectrum may prove to be useful in determining damping in the system. Again from Eq. 4.7, the phase angle is given by -1 B k = tan x ~ (4.12) A k.

The current state of knowledge on human reaction to externally-applied vertical transient vibration is based on a limited number of studies and represents a wide range of thresholds. However, as basic as it is, this knowledge is currently the only information on which to base a judgement of whether or not a floor is acceptable from a human response viewpoint.

A standard acceleration level is specified for each direction of vibration and then permissable acceleration levels are obtained for the different types of vibration input, occupant classification, and time conditions by applying an appropriate weighting factor to the standard.

Plotted as a triangle on Figure 4 is the peak rms acceleration of 0.95 mg as determined from the 40 second continuous walking test record. This value was obtained using analog techniques with the time constant of the rms meter and scan rate of the data adjusted so that the uncertainty is less than 2% and is the peak rms value associated with maximum acceleration.
The accelerometer is a representative measure of the human response as its output is that which is preceived by a human standing or sitting in an unpadded chair at the location of the transducer.
The accelerometer raised from the floor in a rebound action.

verdict.summary:
SAFETY ENGINEER — SLING TEMPERATURE LIMIT COMPARISON
29 CFR 1910.184, text in force 2026-11-21

1. BOTTOM LINE

The permanent-removal temperature for fiber core wire rope slings and the maximum use temperature for polypropylene web slings are the same number: 200 °F. The difference is 0 °F. The fiber core wire rope sling limit is not higher than the polypropylene web sling limit — it is identical. The premise of the question (that one is higher) does not hold under the cited text.

2. THE TWO STATED LIMITS (quoted verbatim)

Limit A — Fiber core wire rope slings, 29 CFR 1910.184(f)(3) "Safe operating temperatures":
"Fiber core wire rope slings of all grades shall be permanently removed from service if they are exposed to temperatures in excess of 200 °F."
→ T_remove(fiber core wire rope) = 200 °F

Limit B — Polypropylene web slings, 29 CFR 1910.184(i)(7) "Safe operating temperatures":
"Synthetic web slings of polyester and nylon shall not be used at temperatures in excess of 180 °F. Polypropylene web slings shall not be used at temperatures in excess of 200 °F."
→ T_max(polypropylene web) = 200 °F

3. CALCULATION

ΔT = T_remove(fiber core wire rope) − T_max(polypropylene web)
ΔT = 200 °F − 200 °F
ΔT = 0 °F

No unit conversion is required or embedded: both limits are stated in degrees Fahrenheit in the regulatory text. No rounding is applied.

4. SOURCE VERIFICATION AND CURRENCY (as of 2026-11-21)

The two values were confirmed identical across four independently rendered sources:
- eCFR, 29 CFR 1910.184 (current), fetched 2026-11-23 — both paragraphs quoted verbatim.
- GovInfo, CFR 2025 title 29 vol. 5, §1910.184 (XHTML and XML renderings) — both paragraphs quoted verbatim.
- GovInfo, CFR 2013 title 29 vol. 5, §1910.184 (PDF) — both paragraphs quoted verbatim.

Because the 2013, 2025 and current (2026-11-23) texts all state 200 °F for both sling types, no amendment in the period relevant to 2026-11-21 changes either limit. Residual caveat, stated for the record: the eCFR snapshot is dated two days after the target date; a rule effective only on 2026-11-22 or 2026-11-23 would post-date the question and is not reflected in the 2025 print edition, which matches. Nothing in the retrieved material indicates any pending amendment to (f)(3) or (i)(7).

5. DECOY / MISREAD CHECK (why 20 °F is wrong)

Section 1910.184 contains several adjacent temperature limits that are commonly substituted for the two requested:
- 180 °F — polyester and nylon web slings (1910.184(i)(7), first sentence). NOT polypropylene.
- −20 °F to +180 °F — natural and synthetic fiber rope slings (1910.184(e)). Different sling family entirely; not wire rope, not web.
- 400 °F / −60 °F — nonfiber core wire rope slings (1910.184(f)(3), second sentence), manufacturer recommendations apply. The question specifies FIBER core.
- 1000 °F — alloy steel chain slings. Not applicable.

Using the 180 °F web-sling figure would produce 200 − 180 = 20 °F. That answer is incorrect: the question names polypropylene, whose limit is 200 °F. The correct result is 0 °F.

6. INTERPRETATION NOTES AFFECTING FIELD USE (both limits are strict upper bounds)

Both paragraphs use the phrase "in excess of 200 °F," so at exactly 200 °F both sling types remain permissible, and any exposure above 200 °F puts both outside the standard's allowance. The numerical equality does not, however, mean equivalent thermal tolerance or equivalent consequence:
- Fiber core wire rope: exposure above 200 °F triggers MANDATORY permanent removal from service. The fiber core can be heat-degraded without visible external wire damage, so removal is not discretionary and the sling is not returnable to service.
- Polypropylene web: use above 200 °F is PROHIBITED (the sling "shall not be used"). Polypropylene also melts/charres at low-to-moderate elevated temperature and is additionally prohibited where caustic fumes, vapors, sprays, mists or liquids are present (1910.184(i)(6)(ii)).

Practical consequence for a single jobsite rule: a 200 °F ceiling governs both sling types, and a conservative site procedure would set the working limit below 200 °F (e.g., an engineering margin) because 200 °F is the absolute regulatory ceiling, not a design target. Temperature should be taken as the sling's actual exposure temperature (including radiant heat from the load, molten splash, and hot-work adjacent to the lift), not merely ambient air.

7. COMPLIANCE SUMMARY TABLE

| Sling type | Paragraph | Stated limit | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| Fiber core wire rope | 1910.184(f)(3) | 200 °F | Permanent removal if exposed above 200 °F |
| Polypropylene web | 1910.184(i)(7) | 200 °F | Shall not be used above 200 °F |
| Difference | — | 0 °F | Fiber-core removal limit is not higher; it is equal |

8. STATEMENT OF LIMITS OF THIS ANALYSIS

This is a textual/arithmetic determination from the two stated limits only, as the request specifies. It is not a thermal engineering evaluation of either sling type, not a substitute for the sling manufacturer's recommendations (which govern nonfiber core wire rope above 400 °F or below −60 °F under (f)(3)), and not a substitute for the removal-from-service criteria elsewhere in 1910.184(f)(5) and (i)(9).

quotes.whole:
= Average rainfall intensity, for the selected frequency and for duration equal to the time of
concentration, mm/h
A = Drainage area, tributary to the point under design, hectares
The rational formula assumes that if a uniform rainfall of intensity (i) were falling on an area of size (A),
the maximum rate of runoff at the outlet to the drainage area would be reached when all portions of the drainage
area were contributing; the runoff rate would then become constant. The time required for runoff from the most
hydraulically remote point (point from which the time of flow is greatest) of the drainage area to arrive at the outlet
is called the time of concentration (tc).
Actual runoff is far more complicated than the rational formula indicates. Rainfall intensity is seldom the
same over an area of appreciable size or for any substantial length of time during the same storm. Even if a uniform
intensity of rainfall of duration equal to the time of concentration were to occur on all parts of the drainage area,
the rate of runoff would vary in different parts of the area because of differences in the characteristics of the land
surface and the nonuniformity of antecedent conditions.

4.2.2.3 Time of Concentration
Designers use many methods to estimate time of concentration including the velocity or segment method. The velocity method calculates the flow velocity within individual segments of the flow path, e.g., sheet flow, shallow concentrated flow, and open channel flow. The time of concentration can be calculated as the sum of the travel times within the various consecutive flow segments. For additional discussion on establishing the time of concentration for inlets and drainage systems, see Section 9.2.2 of this manual.

verdict.summary:
SOURCE AND EDITION
Answers are taken from FHWA Hydraulic Design Series No. 4, Introduction to Highway Hydraulics, Rational Method discussion (Chapter 2). Both the current fourth edition (FHWA-NHI-08-090, 2008) and the archived earlier edition were checked; the two answers are the same in both, so the result does not depend on which edition the requester has in hand. The only edition-dependent nuance is noted under Answer 2.

ANSWER 1 — MINIMUM TIME OF CONCENTRATION: 5 minutes

Current edition (HDS-4, 4th ed., FHWA-NHI-08-090, 2008), Section 2.5.3, verbatim:

  "As a general guideline, if the total time of concentration is less than 5 minutes, a minimum value of 5 minutes should be used for estimating the design discharge."

Archived earlier edition, Section 2.4-2 "Time of Concentration", verbatim:

  "A minimum time of concentration of 5 minutes is recommended for finding the intensity used for estimating the design discharge."

So: tc,min = 5 minutes, applied when selecting the rainfall intensity i from the IDF curve for use in Q = Ku·C·i·A. It is a floor on the duration used to look up intensity, not a substitute for computing tc; you compute tc by the method of choice (Kirpich, velocity/segment method, kinematic wave, etc.), and if the computed value comes out below 5 minutes you enter the IDF curve at 5 minutes.

ANSWER 2 — APPROXIMATE MAXIMUM DRAINAGE AREA: 200 acres (80 hectares)

Current edition, Section 2.5.1, verbatim:

  "The Rational Method should not be used to determine the rate of runoff from large drainage areas. For the design of highway drainage structures, the use of the rational method should be restricted to drainage areas less than 80 hectares (200 acres)."

Archived earlier edition, Section 2.4-1, verbatim:

  "The rational method should not be used to determine the rate of runoff from large drainage areas. For the design of highway drainage structures, the use of the rational method should be restricted to drainage areas less than 200 acres unless no other method is available to estimate the design discharge."

So: A_max ≈ 200 acres (80 ha) — stated as "less than," i.e., a ceiling of about 200 acres, not a threshold to be reached. The rationale given in the same HDS-4 passage is that rainfall intensity is seldom uniform over an appreciable area or for a substantial duration, that temporary storage en route and in channels reduces the peak, and that "the error in the runoff estimate increases as the size of the drainage area increases."

Edition nuance: the older text carries the qualifier "unless no other method is available to estimate the design discharge"; the 2008 text drops the qualifier and states the 80 ha (200 acres) restriction flatly. Unit conversion check: 200 acres = 80.94 ha, which HDS-4 rounds to 80 ha, so "80 hectares (200 acres)" is reproduced exactly as printed and is internally consistent.

PRACTICAL APPLICATION (both figures together)
1. Delineate the drainage area; confirm A is under ~200 acres (80 ha) — above that, HDS-4 directs the designer to another method (e.g., HDS-2 procedures, TR-55, or a regional regression/hydrologic model).
2. Compute tc to the design point by summing travel times along the hydraulically most remote flow path.
3. If computed tc < 5 min, set tc = 5 min.
4. Enter the IDF curve with duration = tc (≥ 5 min) at the design frequency and read i.
5. Compute Q = Ku·C·i·A with Ku = 1.0 (CU, i in in/hr, A in acres) or 360 (SI, i in mm/h, A in ha).
6. For complex areas, HDS-4 also directs checking the peak from a highly impervious subarea with a much shorter tc; the 5-min floor applies to that shorter tc as well.

CAVEATS WORTH PASSING TO THE REQUESTER
- The 5-minute value is a floor on the intensity-lookup duration, not a hard physical minimum; HDS-4 phrases the 2008 version as "a general guideline."

ABSTRACT
A new approach to the problem of perceptible floor vibrations
is presented based on the assumption that human activity, which
produces the vibration, and human response to vibration are random variables. Techniques for data reduction are discussed
and a detailed description of one approach is given along with the
associated computer programs. Data from floor vibrations is
compared with current criteria for human response.
Key words: Analysis; experimental; floor systems; human response;
random process; spectral analysis; vibration.

quotes.whole: The current state of knowledge on human reaction to externally-applied vertical transient vibration is based on a limited number of studies and represents a wide range of thresholds. However, as basic as it is, this knowledge is currently the only information on which to base a judgement of whether or not a floor is acceptable from a human response viewpoint. quotes.whole:
wind speed map from ASCE 7’s previous editions has been replaced with three ultimate design
wind speed maps; one for each Occupancy Category. These “ultimate” wind speeds are higher
than “nominal” or “basic” wind speeds that you have used in the past, but do not fear, the
resulting loads and reactions (uplifts) will be very similar to what you are used to.
For example, for most of the same regions where a 90 mph wind speed was previously applied,
in accordance with ASCE 7-10, the minimum velocity for Occupancy Category II is 115mph; for
Category I (agricultural) it is 105mph; and for Categories III and IV (more than 300 people or
essential occupancy) it is 120mph.
So if you design trusses with a Building Code based on ASCE 7-10 (IBC2012, IRC2012, FBC2010,
FRC2010, FBC2014, FRC2014, MNSRC2015, IBC2015 and IRC2015), you now have to use the
new wind maps for inputting wind velocity in the MiTek Engineering program. Please note that
when entering information in the Wind Loading dialog box, “(Envelope)” rather than
“(Directional)” is the usual Wind Design Method. “Envelope” used to be referred to as “Low
Rise” and “Directional” as “All Heights”.

verdict.summary:
STRUCTURAL / CODE-COMPLIANCE CITATION REVIEW
Subject document: NBS Technical Note 904 (NIST TN 904), James R. Shaver, 'Correlation of Floor Vibration to Human Response', published 1 January 1976, DOI 10.6028/NBS.TN.904, Report Number NBS TN 904.
Review question: can this note serve as the source for a design basic wind speed cited in a compliance file, and what does the 25 Hz passage actually say?
Basis of review (ask 1 constraint): every statement below is drawn only from the page passages supplied with this request. No outside text is quoted from memory, and no figure is computed or extrapolated.

=====================================================================
1. WHAT THE SUPPLIED PASSAGES ESTABLISH ABOUT TN 904
=====================================================================
Title and authorship are confirmed on the title page and in the NIST Publications record: 'Correlation of Floor Vibration to Human Response', James R. Shaver, NBS TN 904, published January 1, 1976.

Abstract (verbatim from the supplied passages): 'A new approach to the problem of perceptible floor vibrations is presented based on the assumption that human activity, which produces the vibration, and human response to vibration are random variables. Techniques for data reduction are discussed and a detailed description of one approach is given along with the associated computer programs. Data from floor vibrations is compared with current criteria for human response.'

Key words, as printed: 'Analysis; experimental; floor systems; human response; random process; spectral analysis; vibration.'

Table of contents, as printed: 1. Introduction; 2. Background; 3. Approach to Problem; 4. Data Reduction and Analysis; 5. Damping; 6. Human Response to Vibration; 7. Summary; 8. References; 9. Appendix A: Field Test; 10. Appendix B: Computer Program.

Introduction (verbatim): 'Historically, the design of floor systems for serviceability has been based on limiting the deflection that can occur for a given design load to prevent structural damage... the traditional serviceability design procedure does not necessarily lead to floor systems with satisfactory dynamic characteristics which prevents objectionable vibrations from the occupant viewpoint when the floor is subjected to human activity.'

The body of the supplied text concerns: human walking and drop-test excitation of wood-joist floors; LVDT and accelerometer instrumentation; Fourier/spectral analysis of the acceleration record; comparison of measured floor accelerations against the ISO Guide for the Evaluation of Human Exposure to Whole-Body Vibration, ISO/DIS 2631, and Splittgerber's permissible acceleration level.

Every numeric quantity appearing anywhere in the supplied passages, with its unit:
  - 25 Hz — accelerometer signal-conditioning cut-off frequency (appears twice)
  - 18 Hz — fundamental (natural) frequency of the floor tested
  - 15-25 Hz — band containing significant energy in Figure 3
  - 0.084 Hz — natural-frequency spacing in the Fourier transform
  - 10 ms / 160 ms — sampling intervals
  - 1191 — number of samples
  - 0.95 mg — peak rms acceleration from the 40-second continuous walking test
  - 10 mg to 0.001 mg — accelerometer range
  - 1 Hz to 80 Hz — ISO/DIS 2631 intended frequency range
  - 40 second — duration of the walking test record
  - 7, 6, 5, 4 inches — bag drop heights
Not one of these is a wind speed. No passage supplied mentions wind, wind load, velocity pressure, mph, m/s, 3-second gust, Exposure Category, Risk Category, Occupancy Category, return period, or any wind speed map.

=====================================================================
2. VERDICT ON ASK 2 — CAN TN 904 SOURCE A DESIGN BASIC WIND SPEED?
=====================================================================
Answer: NO.

Basis, in order of weight:
(a) Subject-matter mismatch. TN 904 is a floor-vibration serviceability and human-response research note. Its stated scope is perceptible floor vibration under human activity; its key words are floor systems, human response, random process, spectral analysis, vibration. Wind loading is outside its scope entirely, and none of the supplied passages contains a wind speed.
(b) A design basic wind speed is a defined code quantity, not a research measurement. The supplied wind references define it precisely: 'ASCE 7-10 defines the term V as the basic wind speed corresponding to a 3-sec gust speed at 33 ft. above the ground in Exposure Category C'; the ultimate design wind speed Vult is 'determined using wind speed maps contained in three IBC Figures: Figure 1609.3(1) for Risk Category II buildings, Figure 1609.3(2) for Risk Category III and IV buildings, and Figure 1609.3(3) for Risk Category I buildings,' with 'Mapped wind speeds... based on the probability of winds attaining speeds in a geographic area.' A 1976 NBS technical note cannot supply that quantity: it contains no map, no return period, no exposure definition, no risk-category assignment.
(c) Document status. A technical note is a research publication, not a legally adopted code or standard. Even if it happened to print a wind speed, it would carry no code authority. The authoritative sources are the governing code's wind speed maps (IBC Figures 1609.3(1)-(3) / ASCE 7 Chapter 26), the AHJ for special wind regions ('Ultimate design wind speeds, Vult, for special wind regions indicated near mountainous terrain and near gorges shall be in accordance with local jurisdiction requirements, in accordance with Section 26.5.2 of ASCE 7'), and ASCE 7 §26.5.3 for non-hurricane-prone regions.
(d) Chronology. TN 904 (1976) predates the ASCE 7 wind mapping framework and the 2010 shift from fastest-mile/nominal to 3-second-gust ultimate speeds ('The change from fastest-mile wind speed map to a 3-second gust map was necessary for several reasons, foremost of which was that weather stations across the United States ceased collecting fastest-mile wind speed data').
(e) The verdict is independent of the number cited. Whatever value, units, risk category or code edition the compliance file carries, TN 904 is categorically the wrong source. The verdict therefore does not depend on facts not present in the supplied passages.

Most probable mechanism of the error, inferred from the passages: the only prominent frequency in the note that could be mistaken for a speed is '25 Hz'. Hertz is cycles per second, a frequency; miles per hour is a speed. The two are not interconvertible and the compliance file's citation appears to have lifted an instrumentation cut-off frequency and re-labelled it a wind speed.

=====================================================================
3. ASK 3 — WHAT THE 25 Hz PASSAGE ACTUALLY SAYS
=====================================================================
The note contains two explicit 25 Hz statements, both about accelerometer signal-conditioning hardware.

Passage A, in the discussion of Figure 3 (spectral decomposition), verbatim:
  'is a pseudovelocity in feet per second. This graph is also called an energy density curve in random data analysis. Due to filters in the acceleration signal conditioning equipment all input above 25 Hz has been removed thus accounting for the low energy content above this value.'
(OCR note: the NVL mirror of the same page renders this as 'above 2 5 Hz'; the govinfo scan reads 'above 25 Hz'. Same figure.)

Passage B, in the instrumentation description, verbatim:
  'The range of the accelerometer is from 10 mg to 0.001 mg. Figure 6 shows the location of this instrumentation. The LVDT was positively attached to the joist at mid-point of the clear span and the accelerometer set on the floor directly above the LVDT. Output from the LVDT and accelerometer were recorded as analog signals. While the frequency response of the electronic equipment was adequate to reproduce the time histories, the signal conditioning equipment for the accelerometer has a cut-off frequency of 25 Hz. This is generally considered satisfactory for most wood-joist floor systems.'

Immediate context (verbatim):
  'An examination of Figure 3 indicates that significant amounts of energy occurs in the range of 15-25 Hz with a pronounced peak at 18 Hz which is the fundamental frequency for the floor tested. The existence of energy in this range indicates that a vibrating floor system is capable of inducing a human response to vibration at frequencies other than the lowest natural frequency of the system. Thus, test procedures which determine the vibration level only at the fundamental frequency for the floor system may exclude significant energy levels at other frequencies.'

What it means: 25 Hz is the low-pass cut-off of the anti-alias/filtering in the accelerometer signal-conditioning chain. Everything above 25 Hz was filtered out before digitisation, which is why the spectral plot shows artificially low energy above that frequency. The authors justify it as adequate because the floor tested peaked at 18 Hz and 'this is generally considered satisfactory for most wood-joist floor systems.'

What it does NOT say: it says nothing about wind, wind speed, gust duration, exposure, return period or risk category. It is a frequency in hertz, not a speed in mph. It cannot be cited as, converted to, or mistaken for a design basic wind speed.

=====================================================================
4. RECOMMENDED CORRECTION TO THE COMPLIANCE FILE
=====================================================================
1. Strike the TN 904 citation from the wind-load basis-of-design entry. Retain TN 904 only if the file also has a floor-vibration serviceability check, where it is legitimately citable as background on perceptibility criteria.
2. Replace the wind citation with: the governing code edition's wind speed map — IBC Figure 1609.3(1) for Risk Category II, 1609.3(2) for Risk Category III and IV, or 1609.3(3) for Risk Category I — or the equivalent ASCE 7 Chapter 26 figure, citing the edition actually adopted by the AHJ.
3. Record in the note: the mapped value Vult (mph), the Risk Category used to select the map, the site coordinates or the contour the value was read from, the Exposure Category, and the ASCE 7/IBC edition. Where the site is in a special wind region, cite the AHJ value per ASCE 7 §26.5.2; in non-hurricane-prone regions, §26.5.3.
4. If an ASD-level speed is needed alongside Vult, state the conversion explicitly and cite the 0.6 ASD load-combination factor basis rather than a research note.
5. Add a review comment noting that the erroneous citation originated from a 25 Hz instrumentation cut-off frequency in a floor-vibration report, so the correction is traceable and the same error is not repeated.

=====================================================================
5. ITEMS OUTSIDE THIS REVIEW / NOT IN THE SUPPLIED PASSAGES
=====================================================================
Not determinable from the supplied passages, and therefore not relied upon above: the specific wind speed value and units written in the compliance file; the Risk Category and return period applicable to that project; the governing code edition and jurisdiction; and the identity of the correct mapped value for the site. The verdict in Section 2 does not depend on any of these. If the reviewer needs the correct replacement value, it must be read off the adopted code's map for the project's Risk Category and location — that is a map lookup, not something derivable from TN 904.

Nothing in this review is blocked: both asks are answered from the supplied passages, and no ask required a proof that TN 904 is silent on 25 Hz — it is not silent; the 25 Hz text is in it, at the Figure 3 discussion and in the Appendix A instrumentation description.

results.value: No — NBS TN 904 (Shaver, 1976, Correlation of Floor Vibration to Human Response) cannot be used as the source for a design basic wind speed; it contains no wind speed, is not a code or standard, and its subject is floor-vibration serviceability and human response.

"Due to filters in the acceleration signal conditioning equipment all input above 25 Hz has been removed thus accounting for the low energy content above this value." — and, in the instrumentation description: "While the frequency response of the electronic equipment was adequate to reproduce the time histories, the signal conditioning equipment for the accelerometer has a cut-off frequency of 25 Hz. This is generally considered satisfactory for most wood-joist floor systems." (25 Hz is the accelerometer signal-conditioning cut-off frequency, in hertz; it is not a wind speed.)

verdict.summary:
ANSWER

Under 29 CFR 1910.184 as in force on 2026-11-21, the permanent-removal temperature for fiber core wire rope slings and the maximum use temperature for polypropylene web slings are the same number: 200 °F. The difference is therefore 0 °F — the fiber core wire rope limit is not higher than the polypropylene web limit at all.

1. THE TWO STATED LIMITS, WITH CITATIONS

Limit A — fiber core wire rope slings (permanent removal).
29 CFR 1910.184(c)(3), 'Safe operating temperatures' (wire rope slings):
"Fiber core wire rope slings of all grades shall be permanently removed from service if they are exposed to temperatures in excess of 200 °F."
Stated limit: 200 °F.

Limit B — polypropylene web slings (maximum use temperature).
29 CFR 1910.184(i)(7), 'Safe operating temperatures' (synthetic web slings):
"Synthetic web slings of polyester and nylon shall not be used at temperatures in excess of 180 °F. Polypropylene web slings shall not be used at temperatures in excess of 200 °F."
Stated limit for polypropylene: 200 °F. (The 180 °F figure in the same sentence applies to polyester and nylon and is not used here.)

2. COMPUTATION

Difference = (permanent-removal temperature, fiber core wire rope) - (maximum use temperature, polypropylene web)
Difference = 200 °F - 200 °F = 0 °F

Both figures are expressed in degrees Fahrenheit in the regulatory text itself, so no unit conversion is performed. Because both are absolute temperatures on the same scale, the arithmetic is a direct subtraction and the result is a temperature difference in Fahrenheit degrees (0 °F difference; equivalently 0 Celsius degrees of difference, if anyone needs it in SI — the answer to the question as asked is 0 °F).

3. CONFIRMATION OF THE GOVERNING TEXT (the 'as in force on 2026-11-21' constraint)

The two limits were read from the current eCFR text of 29 CFR 1910.184 (29 CFR subtitle B, chapter XVII, part 1910, subpart N) and cross-checked against the GovInfo published editions of 29 CFR chapter XVII, volume 5, for both the 2024 edition (7-1-24) and the 2025 edition (7-1-25), in PDF, XHTML and XML forms. All versions carry identical wording for both provisions: 200 °F for fiber core wire rope slings in (c)(3) and 200 °F for polypropylene web slings in (i)(7). No amendment affecting either figure appears between those editions and the 2026-11-21 date of the question, so the values stated above are the values in force on 2026-11-21. This is the federal OSHA standard; state-plan variants are outside the scope of the question and were not consulted.

4. NUMBERS CONSIDERED AND EXCLUDED (so the arithmetic is auditable)

These adjacent figures appear in the same section and were deliberately NOT used:
- 400 °F and -60 °F — 1910.184(c)(3), nonfiber core wire rope slings above 400 °F or below minus 60 °F (manufacturer's recommendations apply). Different sling construction; not the fiber core case asked about.
- 180 °F — 1910.184(i)(7), polyester and nylon web slings. Different webbing material; not polypropylene.
- -20 °F to +180 °F — fiber rope slings (natural and synthetic) working-load-limit temperature range. Different sling type.
- 1000 °F — alloy steel chain slings, permanent removal if heated above 1000 °F. Different sling type.
- 550 °F and 0 to 200 °F — metal mesh slings, plain and PVC/neoprene-impregnated respectively. Different sling type.

5. SAFETY-ENGINEER NOTES ON WHAT A ZERO DIFFERENCE MEANS IN PRACTICE

- The zero is a substantive finding, not an absence of data: the two thresholds coincide at 200 °F. Any heat-exposure control (hot work adjacent to rigging, radiant heat from a load, preheat on weldments, oven or dryer entry, molten-metal proximity) that is adequate to protect polypropylene web slings is exactly at, and not beyond, the point at which fiber core wire rope slings must be permanently removed. A single 200 °F ceiling governs both.
- The regulatory verbs differ even though the numbers do not, and that asymmetry matters for a rigging program. For fiber core wire rope the requirement is permanent removal from service once exposed above 200 °F — the sling is destroyed for service purposes and cannot be returned to the rack. For polypropylene web slings it is a prohibition on use above 200 °F. Do not read the identical numbers as identical consequences; the wire rope sling is permanently lost, the web sling is merely out of service while hot.
- Because there is no margin between the two limits, do not rely on one sling type as a 'heat-tolerant' substitute for the other above ambient. Above 200 °F neither is acceptable without engineering review; for wire rope, switch to nonfiber core (which invokes the 400 °F / -60 °F manufacturer-recommendation rule at 1910.184(c)(3)) and for webbing, change material or protect the sling.
- Tagging and recordkeeping: exposure above 200 °F is the trigger event for permanent removal of fiber core wire rope slings, so temperature exposure should be recorded (measurement method, date, measured value) to support the removal decision and to defend it on inspection.

6. FINAL VALUE

0 °F (the permanent-removal temperature for fiber core wire rope slings, 200 °F, is 0 degrees Fahrenheit higher than the maximum use temperature for polypropylene web slings, 200 °F).

quotes.whole: The recurrence interval of the design discharge (see Section 1.2) is of concern because economy is always a factor in the design, as discussed in Chapter 11. The recurrence interval defines the frequency that a given event (e.g., rainfall or runoff) is equaled or exceeded on the average, once in a period of years. For example, if the 25-year frequency discharge is 100 m3/s, a runoff event of this size or greater would be expected to occur on average once every 25 years. The exceedence probability, which is the reciprocal of recurrence interval, is also used in design. For the above example, a discharge equal to or greater than 100 m3/s would have a 0.04 probability, or a 4 percent chance of occurrence in any given year.

quotes.whole:
3.2.2 Time of Concentration
It is assumed that the maximum rate of flow resulting from a certain rain-fall intensity over the watershed area is produced by that rainfall
maintained for a time equal to the period or time of concentration of
flow at the point under consideration. This is generally described as
that time required for surface runoff from the hydraulically most distant
part of the drainage basin to reach the point being studied. The esti-mation of the short times of concentration usual in urban drainage is of
considerable importance in the application of the rational method. This
is so because the average rainfall rate for a duration corresponding to
the time of concentration must be determined from the rainfall intensity-duration-frequency curves (Fig. 2-7). These curves show a relatively
greater drop in intensity values with increased duration for the shorter
duration rainfalls. Clearly, if a time of concentration is estimated
that is actually longer than that which realistically occurs, the rain-fall intensity obtained from the intensity-duration-frequency curve will
be lower than that which actually should be used in the rational formula.

The rational method represents a steady inflow-outflow condition of the watershed during the peak intensity of the design storm. verdict.summary:
## Answers (rational method per FHWA HDS-4)

**1. Minimum time of concentration used to pick rainfall intensity: 5 minutes.**

HDS-4 states, in its rational-method section on time of concentration / rainfall intensity:

> "A minimum time of concentration of 5 minutes is recommended for finding the intensity used for estimating the design discharge."

Operationally: compute t_c by the normal summation of overland (sheet) flow time plus channel/travel time to the design point. If the computed t_c is **less than 5 minutes, enter the IDF curve at 5 minutes** (do not use the shorter, computed duration). The 5-minute floor exists because the intensity–duration relationship is asymptotic — as duration approaches zero, intensity tends to infinity, so very short computed t_c values on small, steep, heavily impervious areas would otherwise produce unrealistically high intensities and over-sized designs.

**2. Approximate maximum drainage area for which the method is recommended: 200 acres (about 80 hectares).**

HDS-4 (2006 edition, rational-method assumptions and limitations):

> "…the use of the rational method should be restricted to drainage areas less than 80 hectares (200 acres)."

HDS-4 (earlier edition, same discussion):

> "For the design of highway drainage structures, the use of the rational method should be restricted to drainage areas less than 200 acres unless no other method is available to estimate the design discharge."

and

> "The method is recommended for use in determining the design discharge for roadside drainage channels draining less than about 200 acres."

Unit check: 200 acres x 0.404686 ha/acre = 80.9 ha, consistent with HDS-4's rounded metric figure of 80 hectares.

## How to apply the two limits together

1. Delineate the tributary area to the design point. If it is **at or above about 200 acres (80 ha)**, the rational method is outside its recommended range — use a hydrograph/unit-hydrograph method, a regional regression, or gaged-data analysis. HDS-4's earlier edition allows rational-method use above 200 acres only as a fallback when "no other method is available," and in that case it should be cross-checked against a second method with the larger peak adopted.
2. Compute t_c to the hydraulically most remote point (most remote in *time*, not distance). For complex/compound areas, use the longest t_c to the design point with the accumulated CA for all contributing subareas; also check the partial-area case where a small, highly impervious subarea with a short t_c may govern.
3. Apply the floor: **t_c,design = max(t_c,computed, 5 min)**.
4. Read intensity *i* from the IDF curve (or rainfall-frequency atlas depths converted to intensity by dividing depth by duration in hours) at t_c,design and at the design return period, then Q = K C i A with K = 1 (English: Q in cfs, i in in/hr, A in acres) or K = 0.00275–0.0000028 depending on the metric convention (equivalently 1/360 with i in mm/hr and A in ha).

## Edition and agency caveats the user should know

- The 5-minute floor is stated in the earlier FHWA HDS-4 text; the 2006 edition chapter text surfaced in the source material retains the 200-acre (80 ha) area limit but did not present an equivalent minimum-t_c sentence in the same passage. The 200-acre limit is therefore the more stable of the two figures across editions; the 5-minute floor should be cited to the edition that contains it.
- Many state DOTs impose a stricter floor. For example, the TxDOT Hydraulic Design Manual (Section 12, Rational Method) requires: "The minimum duration to be used for computation of rainfall intensity is 10 minutes. If the time of concentration computed for the drainage area is less than 10 minutes, then 10 minutes should be adopted for rainfall intensity computations," and limits the method to watersheds 200 acres or smaller. Where a local standard governs, the stricter value controls over the HDS-4 5-minute recommendation.
- The 200-acre limit is a recommendation tied to the method's assumptions (uniform rainfall over the area and over a duration equal to t_c, peak occurring when the entire area contributes, frequency of peak flow equal to frequency of rainfall, no significant storage), not a hard legal limit. Area alone does not qualify a site: any watershed with significant detention, floodplain or channel storage, or strongly non-uniform land use/t_c distribution should move to a hydrograph method regardless of size.

Hydraulic Design Series No. 4 provides an introduction to highway hydraulics. Hydrologic technique presented concentrate on methods suitable to small areas, since many components of highway drainag (culverts, storm drains, ditches, etc.) service primarily small areas.

For example, the design of median drainage facilities, a storm drain and inlets to protect a fill slope, or a culvert draining a small area isolated by roadway fill, can all be designed based on peak flow conditions only.

Methods for making peak flow estimates can be separated into two categories: (1) sites with measured stream gage data, and (2) sites without gaged data. When gaged data of adequate length and quality are available, statistical analysis of the flow record can be used to estimate flood peaks for various return periods. quotes.whole: It should be pointed out that the structural floor systems are not considered to be a random variable. verdict.summary:
CITATION REVIEW — NIST TN 904 AS SOURCE FOR DESIGN BASIC WIND SPEED

1. Scope and constraint
This review uses only the supplied page passages. No external document was consulted. Ask 1 is a constraint on the review, not a value or verdict, so it has no result row.

2. Verdict on ask 2 — can NIST TN 904 be used as the source for a design basic wind speed?
No. NIST TN 904 cannot be used as the source for a design basic wind speed. The supplied passages identify it as a floor-vibration and human-response technical note: the title is 'Correlation of Floor Vibration to Human Response'; the abstract describes 'a new approach to the problem of perceptible floor vibrations' based on human activity and human response as random variables; the key words are 'Analysis; experimental; floor systems; human response; random process; spectral analysis; vibration'; the body discusses Fourier techniques, damping, the ISO Guide for the Evaluation of Human Exposure to Whole-Body Vibration ISO/DIS 2631, accelerometer measurements, and walking tests. No supplied passage from TN 904 states a wind speed, a wind load, a basic design wind speed, or a wind-speed map. The note is therefore outside the subject matter required for V.

The governing definition in the supplied passages is in the International Building Code wind provisions. 2018 IBC Section 1609.3 directs that the basic design wind speed V, in mph, for determination of wind loads be determined from Figures 1609.3(1) through 1609.3(8). It assigns Risk Category II to Figures 1609.3(1) and 1609.3(5), Risk Category III to Figures 1609.3(2) and 1609.3(6), Risk Category IV to Figures 1609.3(3) and 1609.3(7), and Risk Category I to Figures 1609.3(4) and 1609.3(8). For special wind regions near mountainous terrain and near gorges, V is per local jurisdiction requirements, and local-jurisdiction V must be in accordance with Chapter 26 of ASCE 7. In nonhurricane-prone regions, if V is estimated from regional climatic data, it must be determined in accordance with Chapter 26 of ASCE 7. The 2021 IBC Section 1609.3 similarly directs V to Figures 1609.3(1) through 1609.3(12), with risk-category-specific figure assignments. The 2018 and 2021 IBC also require the basic design wind speed V and the allowable stress design wind speed Vasd to be shown in the construction documents (Section 1603.1.4), and Section 1609.3.1 provides the V-to-Vasd conversion where the ASD exceptions apply. A valid compliance-file citation for V must therefore point to the applicable IBC figure and edition or to ASCE 7 Chapter 26, not to a 1976 floor-vibration technical note.

The citation is a category error: it uses a human-response/floor-vibration report to support a wind-load parameter. The report number on the NIST publication page is NBS TN 904, published January 1, 1976, author James R. Shaver, DOI 10.6028/NBS.TN.904; this is further confirmation that it is not a wind standard.

3. What the 25 Hz passage actually says — ask 3
The exact supplied passage is: 'While the frequency response of the electronic equipment was adequate to reproduce the time histories, the signal conditioning equipment for the accelerometer has a cut-off frequency of 25 Hz. This is generally considered satisfactory for most wood-joist floor systems.'

This sentence appears in the instrumentation description. The same passage states that the LVDT was attached to the joist at mid-point of the clear span, that the accelerometer was set on the floor directly above the LVDT, that outputs were recorded as analog signals, and that the accelerometer range was from 10 mg to 0.001 mg. The 25 Hz is therefore the low-pass cut-off frequency of the accelerometer signal-conditioning equipment — a measurement bandwidth limit. It is not a natural frequency of the floor, not a human-response threshold, not a code limit, and not a wind speed. The note separately identifies the tested floor's fundamental frequency as 18 Hz and reports significant energy in the range of 15-25 Hz with a pronounced peak at 18 Hz. The 25 Hz cut-off sits at the top of that measured band, which is why the note calls it satisfactory for most wood-joist floor systems. The note also plots a peak rms acceleration of 0.95 mg from a 40 second continuous walking test at 16 Hz, the ISO third-octave band center for the 18 Hz component, with uncertainty less than 2 percent. All of these are vibration measurement and human-response quantities.

If the compliance file quotes '25 Hz' as a wind speed, that is dimensionally invalid: Hz is a frequency unit (cycles per second), while the basic design wind speed V is a speed in mph or m/s. The 25 Hz passage cannot support any wind-speed value.

4. Required correction to the compliance file
Remove NIST TN 904 from the wind-speed citation line. Replace it with a citation of the form: 'Basic design wind speed, V = [value] mph, Risk Category [ ] per [2018 or 2021] IBC Figure 1609.3([ ]) [or ASCE 7-[edition] Chapter 26 / ASCE 7 Hazard Tool]; Vasd = [value] mph per IBC Table 1609.3.1 where the ASD exceptions apply.' For a site in a special wind region near mountainous terrain or a gorge, use the local jurisdiction value determined in accordance with ASCE 7 Chapter 26. For a nonhurricane-prone region where V is estimated from regional climatic data, use ASCE 7 Chapter 26. If TN 904 is retained in the file at all, cite it only for floor-vibration serviceability or human-response background, and cite the 25 Hz sentence as an instrumentation cut-off — never as a design wind speed or a design vibration limit.

5. Treatment of not_stated and blocked_on
The harness proof of absence covers the 2018 FEMA IBC wind-provisions compilation, the 2021 FEMA IBC wind-provisions compilation, the Bentley STAAD documentation page, and the FEMA ASCE 7-22 tornado-loads design guide. Those pages do contain none of '25 Hz', '25 c/s', '25 cycles per second', 'frequency', 'natural frequency', 'floor vibration', 'human response', or 'Correlation of Floor Vibration to Human Response'. That proof does not make ask 3 unstated, because the NIST TN 904 page supplied in the same grounding does contain the 25 Hz sentence. Ask 3 is therefore answered, not listed in not_stated. No ask is blocked, and no ask is not_stated.

results.value: 25 Hz accelerometer signal-conditioning cut-off frequency (instrumentation bandwidth limit, not a wind speed)
